title: J&K, Ladakh L-Gs meet Amit Shah in New Delhi - The Tribune
content:
Lieutenant Governors of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh held separate meetings with Union Home Minister Amit Shah in New Delhi on Sunday, officials said. In a post on X, the Ministry of Home Affairs said Shah met J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha and Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena. Saxena said it was an honour to call on the Union Home Minister and apprised him of ongoing developmental projects in Ladakh. “Apprised him of the ongoing developmental projects in Ladakh and sought his valuable guidance for the region’s progress, security and welfare of its people,” he said in a post on X. “Grateful for the constant guidance of Hon’ble HM and unwavering support of the Central Government in fulfilling the aspirations of the people of Ladakh,” he added. As indices lingered near record highs and the market-fear gauge eased, the group that lives closest to the pulse of capital markets found its storyline warming. The annual Jackson Hole symposium has long served as a stage where the tone of monetary matters is set for the months ahead, and this year the message tilted toward a softer stance. With attention drifting away from inflation and toward employment, market participants leaned into the idea that cut has become more likely. For a house tied so closely to capital markets, that shift matters, because cheaper funding tends to loosen the wheels of dealmaking, refinancing, and trading activity that flow through the firm's revenue lines. The change in tone did not arrive in isolation; it landed on a market already reassured by resilient big-technology earnings and a calmer reading on volatility, and the combination gave the banking complex a steadier footing than it had carried during earlier bouts of doubt over the timing of the first move. Banking sits at the crossroads of the broad economy, channeling savings toward the firms and households that put money to work. Within that wide sector, a clear divide separates the deposit-heavy consumer banks from the markets-and-advisory houses that live nearer to Wall Street's dealmaking core. The rate environment shapes both, yet it does so along different channels. For the consumer banks, the spread between deposits and loans dominates; for the markets houses, activity levels across trading and transactions carry the day. Understanding where a firm sits along that spectrum is essential to reading how a shift in the rate path might land, and Goldman Sachs occupies the markets-and-advisory end of the range as clearly as any name in the group. Goldman Sachs occupies a distinctive perch among the largest financial stock firms. Rather than leaning on a vast branch network, the company built its name on advisory work, capital raising, trading, and the management of assets for institutions and wealthy clients. That mix gives the firm a character unlike the sprawling consumer banks, tying performance more directly to the rhythm of markets, the pace of corporate transactions, and the appetite of large clients to move capital. When conditions turn active, the franchise tends to hum, and when they cool, the same sensitivity can cut the other way. The brand carries a weight in boardrooms that few rivals match, an intangible asset built across decades of complex transactions and one that continues to anchor the firm's standing at the center of global dealmaking. At the heart of the company lies its advisory and capital-markets engine, the part of the business that guides corporations through mergers, acquisitions, and the raising of funds through debt and equity. A calmer rate environment often revives boardroom ambition, since executives find it easier to plan large transactions when the cost of money looks steadier. The prospect of easing therefore feeds a storyline in which corporate activity thaws, underwriting desks grow busier, and the advisory pipeline fills. Goldman Sachs has historically ranked among the busiest names in this arena, and any warming of the transaction cycle tends to land squarely in its wheelhouse. The engine feeds on confidence as much as on the cost of money, and a market that reads cut as a step toward a gentler path tends to nurture exactly the kind of confidence that turns tentative talks into completed deals. Alongside advisory work, the firm runs sizable trading operations that span equities, bonds, currencies, and commodities. These desks feed on movement, and a market wrestling with the timing of rate cuts can generate exactly the kind of activity that keeps them engaged. The desks also serve as the connective tissue between the firm and its largest clients, and the relationships they sustain often feed the advisory pipeline in ways that reach well beyond any single quarter's trading revenue. Managing money for institutions, pensions, and affluent households produces revenue that tends to be less jumpy than the swings of trading floors, smoothing the ride across cycles. As rate expectations shifted, the value of a durable, fee-driven business drew fresh appreciation, since it offers ballast when transaction volumes ebb. Building scale here has been a deliberate priority, and the segment now stands as a meaningful counterweight to the more cyclical parts of the house. Rising asset prices, a frequent companion to a gentler rate path, tend to lift the base on which those fees are earned, adding another thread that ties the segment to the broader easing narrative. At the same time, a gentler rate path can compress the spread earned on lending for more traditional banks, which is one reason the market tends to reward the markets-and-advisory model differently from the deposit-and-loan model when easing looms. A markets-focused house also lives with the reality that revenue can swing with sentiment, meaning a quiet stretch for deals or trading can weigh on results. Navigating these crosscurrents while defending market standing is the perennial task, and it grows sharper whenever the rate picture turns uncertain. Goldman Sachs carries relevance well beyond its own results, since the firm often serves as a barometer for the health of dealmaking and the appetite for capital across the market. As the S&P 500 hovered near record highs and easing chatter firmed after Jackson Hole, the firm stood as one lens through which market participants read the tone of the financial complex. For those tracking how the banking group responds to a softening rate path, the company remains a name that captures the interplay of rate expectations, market activity, and the enduring pull of Wall Street's dealmaking machine. title: Attorney general announces indictments in Charleston-area drug trafficking investigation - Live 5 News
content: COLUMBIA, S.C. (WCSC) — South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson announced Monday that a multi-jurisdictional operation was conducted last week to finish apprehending more than 30 individuals indicted in a South Carolina State Grand Jury investigation known as “Last Stand.” Last Stand is focused in the greater Charleston area and grew out of investigations into unsanctioned nightclubs that officials say became hubs for narcotics trafficking, prostitution and gang violence. Indictments against certain defendants were unsealed today after the roundup operations last week. “Narcotics trafficking from Mexican cartels poses a threat to national security, and I commend our partner agencies for doing the difficult and dangerous job of investigating and apprehending alleged gang- and cartel-affiliated individuals,” Wilson said. “This investigation involves not only drug trafficking on a large scale, but also gun smuggling, prostitution and shootings, with illegally operating businesses and nightclubs often being the epicenter of this criminal activity,” he added. Months of surveillance, intelligence gathering, enforcement actions and State Grand Jury investigation led Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Charleston Field Office, the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED), the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO) and other law enforcement partners to perform a state search and seizure warrant at an unsanctioned nightclub in North Charleston in the early morning hours of Sunday, Feb. 8, 2026. That raid led to the arrest of 86 people, including 79 administrative arrests of illegal immigrants and seven criminal arrests. Four trafficking victims were identified, and one juvenile was discovered and turned over to relatives. Firearms, 45 grams of cocaine, crack cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and 347 grams of marijuana were seized during the raid, according to officials. As the investigation continued, it led to the identification of international narco-terrorist cartels and gangs involved in the large-scale trafficking of narcotics predominantly to the Charleston area of South Carolina. According to a release from the South Carolina Attorney General, the trafficking pipeline was historically responsible for hundreds of kilos of cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl brought from cartel sources in Mexico through southern border states and into South Carolina. HSI, SLED, CCSO, the Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office, Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office, Summerville Police Department, South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, South Carolina Department of Corrections Office of Inspector General, and other federal, state and local agencies conducted large-scale enforcement operations in South Carolina, Texas, Georgia and Florida to dismantle the alleged drug trafficking organizations in South Carolina. The latest operations last week resulted in the seizure of several kilograms of narcotics, including cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine. Thirty-three firearms, including multiple machine guns, were also seized by law enforcement. “Today is the direct result of a multi-year, complex and thorough investigation by dedicated public servants, committed to making our state safer,” said SLED Chief Mark Keel. “These organizations bring drugs, guns and violence into our communities, and we’re not going to allow them to operate here unchecked,” said Mark M. Zito, special agent in charge of HSI Carolinas. State Grand Jury Division chief attorney S. Creighton Waters thanked all the partner agencies for their hard work. “Operation Last Stand is State Grand Jury doing what State Grand Jury does best – bringing multi-jurisdictional partnerships together to punch harder together than we ever could individually,” he added. title: This 300-HP Lexus Sleeper Matched BMW Muscle Without The German Repair Bills - HotCars
content: By the late 1990s, the luxury sports sedan had evolved into one of the automotive industry's fiercest battlegrounds. Premium automakers were no longer competing solely on refinement, prestige, or comfort—straight-line performance had become just as important. Yet impressive acceleration figures alone weren't enough to win enthusiast approval. Reputation increasingly depended on something less tangible: how a car made its driver feel. Amid that landscape, one Japanese luxury sedan quietly produced performance numbers comparable to the benchmark BMW 540i, yet never earned the same reputation. Its greatest disadvantage wasn't found beneath the hood or within its chassis, but somewhere far less mechanical. We've updated the article with more details on the evolution of this Lexus luxury sedan. By the time the E39-generation BMW 540i arrived,     BMW had already established itself as the benchmark for building sports sedans that balanced luxury with genuine driver involvement. The 540i refined that formula further by combining a smooth, naturally aspirated V8 with a chassis that felt equally comfortable on a winding back road and a long-distance highway journey. It wasn't the fastest executive sedan of its era, nor the most powerful, but it delivered an experience that felt complete in a way few rivals managed. Much of that reputation stemmed from BMW's decision to offer the 540i with a six-speed manual transmission. At a time when luxury manufacturers were increasingly steering buyers toward sophisticated automatic gearboxes, BMW continued to cater to enthusiasts who valued direct mechanical engagement above outright convenience. The manual-equipped 540i became more than just another drivetrain option—it became central to the car's identity and helped cement its status as the driver's choice within the segment. That timing proved significant because enthusiast culture increasingly equated three pedals with authenticity. Automotive publications praised manual transmissions for the greater sense of involvement they provided, while buyers often viewed them as proof that a manufacturer genuinely prioritized the driving experience. Automatic transmissions had become smoother, more intelligent, and, in many situations, equally capable, but public perception hadn't evolved at the same pace. As a result, any rival hoping to challenge the BMW faced an obstacle extending well beyond measurable performance. Matching its acceleration or handling would not automatically earn the same respect if enthusiasts believed the driving experience itself was compromised. It was against this backdrop that another luxury manufacturer quietly pursued a fundamentally different vision for the modern performance sedan. While much of the segment increasingly embraced the formula that had made German performance sedans so desirable, one manufacturer chose not to chase driver involvement in exactly the same way. Instead of building a car that demanded constant interaction, its engineers focused on delivering effortless performance, exceptional refinement, and the kind of long-term durability that had already become a defining strength of the brand. The objective wasn't to imitate the benchmark—it was to prove there was another path to building a genuinely capable luxury performance sedan. That philosophy shaped the development of a new rear-wheel-drive executive sedan that represented a significant departure from its predecessor. Engineers strengthened the chassis, refined the suspension, sharpened steering response, and improved overall body control, but resisted sacrificing ride quality simply to create a harsher, more aggressive character. The goal remained balance rather than extremity, ensuring the car retained the comfort expected of a premium luxury sedan while becoming noticeably more rewarding to drive. The same thinking extended beneath the hood. Rather than chasing peak horsepower figures alone, engineers concentrated on creating a V8 that delivered broad, effortless torque, exceptional smoothness, and dependable performance over hundreds of thousands of miles. Variable Valve Timing with intelligence (VVT-i) broadened the engine's operating range, while careful calibration prioritized immediate real-world response instead of requiring constant high-rev driving to access meaningful performance. The result reflected an engineering philosophy that valued usable speed over dramatic theater. That approach ultimately produced a luxury sedan capable of matching the segment's established benchmark where objective performance was concerned—even if it arrived there through an entirely different philosophy. That sedan was the Lexus GS 400, introduced as the flagship performance model of the second-generation GS lineup. Rather than attempting to replicate BMW's character, Lexus developed the GS 400 to demonstrate that effortless refinement and genuine performance could coexist without compromise. It wasn't designed to become a track-focused sports sedan or a luxury car with a larger engine. Instead, it embodied Lexus's belief that engineering sophistication could deliver competitive performance while remaining unmistakably Lexus. Power came from a revised 4.0-liter 1UZ-FE V8 equipped with VVT-i, producing 300 horsepower and 310 lb-ft of torque. Paired exclusively with a five-speed electronically controlled automatic transmission driving the rear wheels, the GS 400 recorded 0–60 mph times ranging from approximately 5.7 to 6.0 seconds in contemporary road tests, depending on the publication. Those figures placed it directly alongside the BMW 540i and Mercedes-Benz E420/E430, proving that Lexus had achieved genuine parity where straight-line performance was concerned. The engine's character mattered just as much as its headline figures. With roughly 80 percent of its peak torque available from just 1,800 rpm, the revised 1UZ-FE delivered immediate, seamless acceleration across almost the entire rev range. Rather than encouraging drivers to chase redlines, it produced effortless thrust whether pulling away from traffic lights, merging onto a highway, or overtaking slower vehicles. That broad torque delivery perfectly reflected Lexus' grand touring philosophy, making the GS 400 feel consistently responsive without demanding constant driver effort. The industry's recognition of the 1UZ-FE reinforced that engineering achievement. The V8 earned repeated praise for combining refinement, performance, and durability, including recognition through Ward's 10 Best Engines program during the GS 400's production period. It demonstrated that Lexus hadn't simply built a reliable luxury engine—it had created one of the most sophisticated V8 powerplants of its era. On paper and on the road, the GS 400 had achieved exactly what it set out to do: produce performance capable of running with the BMW 540i through engineering rather than imitation. Despite matching the     BMW 540i in outright performance, the GS 400 never achieved the same standing among driving enthusiasts. The reason had little to do with horsepower, acceleration, or chassis capability. Instead, it came down to a single product decision that shaped public perception from the moment the car arrived in showrooms. Unlike the BMW 540i, which offered buyers the option of a six-speed manual transmission, the GS 400 was available exclusively with a five-speed electronically controlled automatic. Lexus engineered the transmission to prioritize smoothness and refinement, while its E-Shift manual mode allowed drivers to select gears sequentially. For everyday driving, it was quick, unobtrusive, and well matched to the V8's broad torque curve. But to enthusiasts accustomed to equating manual gearboxes with driver involvement, it wasn't enough. Period road tests reflected that contrast. Reviewers consistently praised the GS 400's composure, effortless power delivery, and remarkable refinement, often acknowledging that it could match or closely trail the BMW in objective performance testing. Yet when discussions turned to driver engagement, the conversation almost inevitably returned to the BMW's manual transmission. The ability to choose gears manually with a clutch pedal created a stronger emotional connection, even if it offered little measurable advantage in day-to-day performance. That distinction ultimately shaped how both cars were remembered. The BMW became the enthusiast's benchmark because it delivered not only speed, but also a level of interaction that buyers associated with a true driver's car. The Lexus, meanwhile, was viewed as the more mature and refined alternative—a car that achieved similar results through engineering sophistication rather than mechanical theater. In hindsight, its reputation was influenced less by what it could do than by what it chose not to offer. The second-generation Lexus GS was a major leap over the first-generation car when it debuted in 1998. For the first time in the U.S.-market GS, buyers could get a V8, and the GS 400's 4.0-liter 1UZ-FE arrived with VVT-i, helping transform the sedan into a much more capable performance machine. The new platform was also substantially stiffer and more sophisticated than its predecessor. But the luxury sedan segment was moving fast. An escalating technology race among European rivals, combined with tightening emissions requirements, pushed Lexus to rethink the formula just three years into the second-generation GS's run. In 2001, the GS received a significant mid-cycle refresh. The exterior received a cleaned-up grille, revised lighting, larger exhaust tips, and fresh six-spoke alloy wheels. The cabin received an equally important technology upgrade, with available DVD navigation, standard audio controls on the steering wheel, a compass, improved audio equipment, and new trim details. Lexus also added standard side-curtain airbags and other safety upgrades, pushing the GS further into premium-sedan territory. Yet the biggest change was hiding beneath the bodywork. Lexus replaced the 4.0-liter V8 with a larger engine, bringing the GS 400 nameplate to an end and ushering the performance sedan into its next chapter as the     GS 430. The GS 430's 4.3-liter 3UZ-FE wasn't a clean-sheet engine. Lexus took the proven 1UZ-FE and stretched its displacement the easy way: the stroke stayed at 82.5 mm, while the bore grew from 87.5 to 91.0 mm. The result was 4,293 cc versus 3,969 cc, giving the facelifted sedan more low- and mid-range muscle while helping the V8 satisfy evolving emissions requirements. The headline power figure stayed at 300 hp, but torque rose from 310 to 325 lb-ft, giving the GS 430 stronger low- and mid-range shove. Lexus also refined the engine's control systems, retaining VVT-i while optimizing VVT-i, ACIS and ETCS-i and revising the intake, exhaust, ignition and emissions hardware for a cleaner, smoother and more efficient power delivery. That doesn't mean enthusiasts automatically prefer the newer V8, as some still choose the 1UZ. Its smaller bore and thicker cylinder liners give high-output builders more material to work with, while the 3UZ's larger bore and thinner liners leave less room for aggressive builds. The GS 400's ETCS-i also retained a physical accelerator cable as part of its mechanical fail-safe system, a touch that still appeals to tuners who prefer a more mechanical connection to the throttle. Viewed through a modern lens, the GS 400's philosophy appears surprisingly forward-thinking. Today's high-performance luxury sedans are almost exclusively equipped with sophisticated automatic transmissions, while smooth, effortless torque delivery has become a defining characteristic of the segment. The qualities that once led some enthusiasts to dismiss the Lexus have since become accepted as the industry standard. Its naturally aspirated     1UZ-FE V8 has also earned a reputation for exceptional durability, with numerous examples covering high mileage while retaining the refinement that made the engine so impressive when new. Combined with conservative styling, solid build quality, and a well-balanced rear-wheel-drive platform, the GS 400 has become increasingly appreciated by enthusiasts seeking an understated performance sedan that can still be driven and enjoyed without constant mechanical attention. Perhaps more importantly, time has shifted the conversation away from what the GS 400 lacked and toward what it accomplished. Rather than attempting to imitate BMW's formula, Lexus proved there was another way to build a compelling performance sedan—one that prioritized seamless power delivery, engineering refinement, and everyday usability without sacrificing genuine pace. That philosophy may not have generated the same enthusiast mythology as the manual-equipped 540i, but it produced a car that has aged with remarkable dignity. The GS 400 was never remembered as loudly as its German rival, yet history suggests it deserved greater recognition. It demonstrated that matching the benchmark didn't require copying it, and that intelligent engineering could be just as effective as chasing the traditional enthusiast playbook. Its legacy is therefore defined not by the transmission it never offered, but by how convincingly it proved there was more than one route to building a great V8 sport sedan. title: Vikings Sign Defensive Lineman Jonathan Harris & Tight End Matt Lauter - Minnesota Vikings
content:
EAGAN, Minn. — Two familiar faces are returning to the Vikings. The team announced Monday it signed defensive lineman Jonathan Harris and tight end Matt Lauter. Minnesota waived third-year defensive lineman Taki Taimani and rookie cornerback Tyreek Chappell with injury designations in corresponding moves. The 30-year-old Harris originally signed with Minnesota in December 2024 and spent the 2025 season on the Vikings practice squad before he was released in January of this year. In 40 career games (nine starts), the 6-foot-5, 295-pound Harris has produced 91 tackles, including seven for losses, one sack and seven quarterback hits. Harris recorded the bulk of those stats — 43 tackles and a sack — over 17 games and five starts for Denver in 2023. Harris joined Chicago in 2019 as an undrafted free agent out of Lindenwood, which was a Division-II program at the time, and he stayed with the Bears until late October that season. Harris joined Denver soon thereafter and played 31 games for the Broncos through 2023. Harris also had a brief stint with Miami and made seven appearances for Carolina in 2024. The veteran DL rejoins a room that has added draft picks Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange, plus 28-year-old Isaiahh Loudermilk, among others, since his initial departure. Lauter, a Boise State product, participated in Vikings Rookie Minicamp on a tryout basis in May. He grew up in San Diego, California, where he attended Torrey Pines High School and especially garnered attention during his junior season — recording 20 passes for 316 yards and three touchdowns, in addition to logging 47 tackles, three forced fumbles and an interception on defense. Lauter redshirted as a freshman in 2021 and the next season appeared in all 14 games. During his junior season for the Broncos, Lauter racked up 47 catches for 619 yards and seven receiving touchdowns, which ranked first in the conference and earned him First-Team All-Mountain West honors. He was credited with 381 yards after the catch. Lauter played in 13 games in 2025, making eight starts, and finished the season with 37 receptions for 330 yards and two touchdowns. He finished his collegiate career with 1,146 receiving yards and 12 touchdowns, ranking third all-time among Boise State tight ends. The Raiders signed Lauter as an undrafted free agent on April 30 but waived him two days later. He also was with the Titans briefly this offseason. title: Building a Supercharged Lexus GS 430: First Drive - thetruthaboutcars.com
content: We wrap up a few small but important details on our supercharged 2001 Lexus GS430 before uploading a custom All4Swap tune to the factory ECU so we can experience for the first time what this Range Rover TVS1900 supercharger can really do on the stock 3UZ V8 engine. Speed Academy is a website and YouTube channel based on making things go fast and enjoying cars. Peter Tarach and Dave Pratte are the forces behind Speed Academy. The TTAC Creators Series tells stories and amplifies creators from all corners of the car world, including culture, dealerships, collections, modified builds and more. An AI-produced summary of the transcript, edited by a staffer, is below. Become a TTAC insider. Get the latest news, features, TTAC takes, and everything else that gets to the truth about cars first by  subscribing to our newsletter. The transcript follows the final stages of a $6,000 2001 Lexus GS 430 build, which began life as a clean luxury sedan but has been transformed into a supercharged sleeper with a budget Range Rover supercharger, TRD-style body kit, upgraded suspension, custom headlights and other performance and cosmetic modifications. The goal is to resolve the remaining bugs, load a custom ECU tune and finally see how the car performs. The first job is refinishing the supercharger intake tube. The large logo and chrome finish are replaced with a wrinkle-black VHT coating, giving the engine bay a cleaner, more understated appearance. The paint turns out well despite a small dent and scratch caused by dropping the tube. The team also addresses a check-engine light caused by the EVAP system. Because the modified intake/supercharger setup left an EVAP sensor improperly plumbed, they connect it to a vacuum source between the throttle body and supercharger. They also fix the intercooler heat-exchanger pump, which was receiving constant power from the fuse box even with the ignition off. The solution is to connect it to switched power from the headlight wiring. The GS 430 has custom projector headlights using Q45-style projector lenses, but the existing setup wasn't producing enough light. The car actually had factory wiring for HID headlights, so the team installs an HID system. One bulb turns out to be broken and requires replacement, but once installed, the HIDs produce substantially better illumination. The custom headlights also receive a ceramic sealant to protect their appearance. A major step is loading the All for Swaps custom tune supplied by Brandon at Quantum Auto. Rather than simply sending the ECU away for a one-time flash, the team invests in the necessary PCM Flash cable, dongle and software so the ECU can be modified again in the future if the car receives larger injectors or a higher-boost pulley. Both the TCU and ECU maps are flashed, giving the GS 430 its first opportunity to run at full power. The driver's door has several problems, including an inoperative power mirror and a key-fob locking issue. Inspection reveals no obvious broken wires in the door harness. Cleaning the mirror-switch contacts unexpectedly restores its operation, although the switch itself appears worn and only works reliably when pushed aggressively. The key-fob problem proves more difficult. The wiring is poorly soldered, so it is cleaned up, but that doesn't solve the issue. The team successfully puts the car into key-fob programming mode and establishes communication between the fob and car, yet the locks still don't respond. After roughly 20 attempts at reprogramming, the problem remains unresolved, possibly pointing to a module or another electrical fault. The aftermarket TRD gauge cluster looks impressive, with a 320-km/h speedometer and 9,000-rpm tachometer, but it is badly calibrated for the GS 430's engine. At an actual 100 km/h, for example, it reads approximately 120 km/h. Because the cluster was originally designed for an Aristo and its calibration doesn't match the GS 430's UZ-series engine, there is no simple fix. The team therefore removes it and reinstalls the stock gauge cluster, sacrificing some visual flair for accurate readings. With the ECU/TCU tune installed and the remaining major mechanical work completed, the GS 430 finally gets its first full-power test drive. The supercharged V8 delivers a noticeable increase in performance, with the larger supercharger providing stronger acceleration than the builder's previous LS 430 equipped with a smaller M12 blower. Power delivery is described as smooth, with crisp transmission shifts, although the transmission itself feels somewhat dated. The supercharger whine is audible without overwhelming the exhaust note, giving the car the desired sleeper character. The reviewers are particularly impressed with how quick the GS 430 feels after the tune. The car's Tein Flex Z coilovers with EDFC5 electronic damping control also receive a positive review. The system automatically adjusts damping based on road conditions and information from its accelerometers/G-force sensors and GPS. Despite costing roughly $1,000 for the coilovers and another $700–$800 for the EDFC system, the setup provides a surprisingly comfortable and sophisticated ride. The GS 430 is substantially less floaty than before, yet it remains smooth and planted. It handles normal bumps exceptionally well, although it can crash over particularly severe bumps at high speed. The combination of the suspension and Continental tires significantly improves the car's handling and reduces the body roll that previously made the GS 430 feel like a boat. The project is considered a major success. The supercharged GS 430 combines sleeper looks, substantial power, improved handling and a surprisingly comfortable ride, all while maintaining the character of an old luxury sedan. The builder is especially pleased with the supercharger's sound and performance and considers the car essentially finished. However, the actual horsepower figures have not yet been revealed. A final episode will put the car on a dyno and compare it in a roll race against Pete's BMW M5. Bottom line: What started as a $6,000 2001 Lexus GS 430 has evolved into a genuinely quick, extensively modified sleeper. The build still has a few unresolved electrical quirks, but the important parts — the supercharged powertrain, tune, suspension and overall driving experience — have exceeded expectations. title: Protecting AI Models Alone Is Insufficient… GS Neotek Presents 'Operational Security' Solution - 벤처스퀘어
content: As corporate AI adoption moves beyond the pilot phase into actual business operations and customer services, the scope of security is also changing. It is now necessary to manage not only the performance and safety of the models themselves but also the connected cloud, data, account permissions, code, and workloads as a whole. The capability to integrate regulatory compliance, threat response, and remediation records into a single operating system has also become crucial. GS Neotek has expanded the focus of its cloud MSP business into the AX domain by unveiling a solution that links AI service deployment with security operations. GS Neotek participated in the 'AI Summit Seoul & Expo 2026 (AISE 2026)' held at COEX in Samseong-dong, Seoul, where it demonstrated four types of AI and security solutions and conducted a specialized session on the theme of trusted operation of AI services. Marking its ninth year, the AI Summit Seoul & Expo featured 118 companies from seven countries operating 307 booths. The number of participating companies increased by 66.2% compared to last year. GS Neotek set up an exclusive booth to introduce solutions that support corporate AI adoption, service development, and security operations. The products showcased at the event include the video intelligence 'MediaLens', the AX agent 'aiDea', the cloud security platform 'Security Lens', and the organizational agent operating system 'O2'. MediaLens analyzes video data to automatically generate response reports. AIIDE designs ideas entered by users in natural language into AI services within an on-premises AI environment and connects necessary functions. O2 supports workflows within an organization by integrating existing collaboration tools with AI agents. The solution most prominently featured at the event was 'Security Lens,' a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP) developed in-house by GS Neotek. It manages assets and security risks distributed across multi-cloud and on-premises environments on a single screen, analyzes attack paths between assets, and suggests response priorities. It provides a basic framework for responding to domestic security regulations, such as ISMS-P, and supports threat analysis and remediation tasks using a Korean-based AI agent. It is configured to connect discovered risks to ticket issuance, Service Level Agreement (SLA) management, remediation history, and evidence management, enabling security personnel to manage the entire response process from risk detection to the end. In the specialized session, Park Je-ho, Security Lead at GS Neotek, gave a presentation on the topic of "Trusted Operations of AI Services and Security Risks Outside the Model." Lead Park explained the legal obligations and operational tasks that companies must review in the context of the implementation of the Framework Act on AI, and analyzed the attack surfaces of cloud, authority, data, code, and workloads existing outside of AI models. AI services do not operate solely on the basis of their models. Because data repositories, external APIs, user permissions, application code, and cloud infrastructure are interconnected, a vulnerability in any one area can affect the reliability of the entire service. GS Neotek has presented a security operations framework that goes beyond merely discovering these risks to managing the assignment of responsible personnel, timelines for corrective actions, and response results. GS Neotek has been providing multi-cloud management services based on its top partner status with AWS and Google Cloud. The company plans to leverage its MSP consulting experience, which encompasses AI, cloud, AICC, CDN, and security, to support enterprises from the development of AI services to infrastructure construction, regulatory compliance, and security operations. "This event provided practical solutions to implementation, reliability, and security—the biggest concerns for companies during the AI adoption process," said Seo Jeong-in, Head of the IT Business Division at GS Neotek. "Based on our accumulated cloud MSP consulting capabilities, we aim to establish ourselves as an integrated partner that supports customers' AI transformation and the establishment of secure security systems." AI, which used to generate reports and interact with customers, is now picking up and transporting goods and infiltrating factory equipment and operations. As the number of tasks entrusted to AI increases, corporate interests have naturally shifted. title: Mailbag: Reviewing Vikings Week vs. Ravens; Young Defensive Linemen Noticed by Fans - Minnesota Vikings
content:
Do you have a comment or question? Send it to the Mailbag. Every Monday we'll post several comments and/or questions. Click here to submit a comment or question to Mailbag. Remember to include your name and town in the email. If Twitter / X is your jam, you can send a question to me that way as well. The Vikings hosted their lone home preseason game Saturday and fell 13-3 to the Ravens, but the big-picture item of the week was the feeling of having accomplished several items and identifying others to work on during the two joint practices between Minnesota and Baltimore. In my years of covering joint practices, I'd say the defenses for both teams usually win the first day, which is not dissimilar from the first day of padded training camp practices each year (that happened again this year at Vikings camp). Such was the case Wednesday, except for the 2-minute drill in which Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy each led touchdown drives. Minnesota's offense evened things out a bit more on Thursday while its defense remained dominant. Even though it was truly great to return to U.S. Bank Stadium Saturday for the first time since Week 18 on Jan. 4, the game action felt a little bit anticlimactic because of a couple ups and downs for McCarthy, who got the start with the second-team offense. McCarthy did a great job of feeling pressure, climbing the pocket and giving Tai Felton a great opportunity on a 50-50 ball that went for 50. But the QB with 10 career regular-season starts under his belt lamented execution in the red zone on a second-and-goal pass from the 3 and a fourth-and-goal from the 1. On the other side of the ball, rookies Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange relished their first opportunity at U.S. Bank Stadium, as well as another opportunity to advance their development with meaningful snaps. Minnesota will close its preseason by visiting Denver at 8 p.m. (CT) Friday. Before we get to some questions, I'd like to say it was such a treat to welcome Hub Meeds and his family to the Minnesota Vikings Museum on Thursday. Meeds visited dressed in regalia befitting what he wore on the sidelines as the team's live mascot for more than two decades (1970-92). Meeds' iconic look originated at Super Bowl IV when he and his brother-in-law, Dan Jeans, rented costumes before heading to New Orleans. Meeds, a White Bear Lake truck driver, and Jeans, a St. Paul hair stylist, had tickets to the game, but approached a player gate at Tulane Stadium. Officials mistakenly let them onto the field. Meeds, who had played football at Stillwater High School, liked the view from the sidelines and asked the Vikings if he could become the team's mascot. He was with the team in an official capacity at their next three Super Bowls. Meeds worked home games until 1992 and attended the final game at the Metrodome. After first using a fake beard, Meeds grew the real deal. He also found a 36-inch sword that was made in Germany in 1888 and fashioned a shield. The sword and shield are on display at the Museum in an area that pays tribute to Metropolitan Stadium. Meeds' iconic look was even featured as the cover of the team's 1973 media guide, which happens to be one of the ones mounted on the pillar of Vikings.com's assigned area in the press box. Viktor the Viking, who launched in 2007, was excited to meet Meeds at the Minnesota Vikings Museum. Both enjoyed posing for pictures with guests, and it was wonderful to see multiple generations of Vikings fans connecting at the exhibits. Vikings fans have shown their enthusiasm and devotion to the team in a variety of ways, including the way they dress for home and away games, further linking themselves to their team. Lastly, I'll note that everyone should be on the lookout tomorrow for the unveiling of the Vikings Rivalries uniforms, which will be worn by the team for the first time on Dec. 20 when Minnesota hosts the Detroit Lions. View game action photos from the Vikings preseason game vs. the Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium. Two preseason games in the books. For the second consecutive week, the second unit offensive line was bad. Nothing to write home about. Ground game couldn't get going, six pressures allowed on 11 dropbacks for McCarthy, and another crippling penalty that wiped out a first down. When opportunity was there, McCarthy continued to miss. Four open receivers he couldn't hit. Still throwing too hard and too high. The defense on the other hand looked very good. Tyler Huntley is a very experienced and quality backup QB. He looked awful and very uncomfortable. The D-line looks to have very strong depth. Banks and "Big Citrus" both looked much more settled into NFL football. One game left to get it together. What are the dates for roster cuts? Do they have to cut to 53 in one shot, or is it still broken up through camp? — Roman B., counting down the days until kickoff against Green Bay from Grand Forks, North Dakota In a couple of aspects, Saturday's game reminded me a bit of last year's regular-season game against the Ravens. The reasons were beyond the plentiful purple and centered on McCarthy's day. Both games featured a completion of 50-plus yards by McCarthy, as well as some misses on passes he wishes were completed. Both games also included some leaks along the offensive line. In the regular season last November, the Ravens racked up 12 QB hits on McCarthy. On Saturday, the group hit him four times across Minnesota's final two possessions of the first quarter, including a couple at the knee or below (no flags were thrown on either). One of those hits occurred when he stayed in the pocket and uncorked a beautiful pass to Jeshaun Jones for a gain of 19 on a third-and-13, but the positive was erased because of a holding penalty against Henry Byrd, who has worked at tackle this season after spending earlier seasons on the interior. No one on social media is pointing out that execution by McCarthy. With the Vikings resting starting tackles Christian Darrisaw and Brian O'Neill, and rookie Caleb Tiernan working his way back from an ankle injury in the preseason opener, the Vikings opted to start veteran Ryan Van Demark at right tackle and Byrd at left tackle. Both defenses stymied the ground game. There was only one run the entire game for 10 or more yards (a 15-yarder for Jermar Jefferson who finished with two carries for 15 yards), so that didn't help any quarterback who played. I'm in the camp that McCarthy has improved certain aspects of his game this offseason, but the Vikings didn't establish the running game the way they did early at New York, and the protection didn't hold for McCarthy on some passes. The play that has generated the most alacrity on social media is the missed throw on fourth-and-goal from the 1. There's a bit of nuance that has been left out. The outside linebacker for the Ravens, Ethan Burke, is 6-foot-6 with 33-inch arms and synched his jump to maximize its effect thanks to a little hitch at the top of the drop by McCarthy. That pressure caused a high throw out of reach of Price. I'm not going to pretend to be a coach, but perhaps a quicker release (before the defender can get his arms up or a pump fake and then release after the OLB lands might have helped a better outcome. I'm also quite bullish on the long-term combination of Banks and Orange, especially in the context of a really encouraging group of players that also includes Jalen Redmond and Levi Drake Rodriguez, a pair of absolute hosses. Banks and Orange were drafted where they were because of some pretty incredible traits that are fun for Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores to add to his concoction. The deadline for teams to reduce their rosters from 90 to 53 is 5 p.m. (CT) on Sunday, Aug. 30, but reductions could happen at any point between Friday's preseason finale and that deadline. Teams could make claims on players subject to the waiver process, so there could be some more fluidity. Practice squads of up to 17 (if one is an International Player) can then be formed next Monday. I have to admit I felt a little sick to my stomach with Minnesota's effort against Baltimore, but then I felt better after I saw that a bunch of starters didn't suit up. So it was second and third stringers trying to make an impression ahead of cutdown days. Although I wondered if it was fourth and fifth stringers manning the o-line. They do realize they're not playing Pop Warner, right? There's no participation trophies in the NFL. Even so, did the QBs have to act like a pillar of strength, or a mannequin? Isn't that why they have legs? But I'm guessing the Vikings may not be able to keep four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster, so the odd man out will have to hope they get signed to the practice squad or another team. But I'm pretty sure the team invested too much in J.J., so I doubt they'll release him. Which means Wentz or Brosmer will draw the short straw. But with roster cuts coming up, I don't know what the numbers are and when they fall, but there's just one preseason game left, so who looks like they've put in the extra effort to survive the first or second cuts? And has Hitman Harry officially hung up his cleats, or is his protracted indecision causing anxiety for rookies in the secondary? After the game and watching the highlights I do feel a bit queasy. And September is just around the corner, so for those who want to be wearing Purple come December, or eternally hopeful for late January and February, they need some urgency and some "dawg" in their play style. — David A. (from the North Shore but melting in the South) I mentioned Minnesota's thinness of experienced players at tackle in the above answer. In addition to sacking McCarthy once, the Ravens dropped Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer twice each and totaled nine QB hits. That's less than ideal when trying to give McCarthy and Brosmer developmental reps. It's accurate to categorize Wentz as a known commodity, given his 99 career regular-season starts that included five with Minnesota in 2025. Head Coach Kevin O'Connell was disappointed with nine penalties, including six on offense that seemed to undermine the establishment of rhythm in Saturday's game. The Vikings have had their depth at safety tested, with Jakobe Thomas experiencing back tightness for multiple weeks and with Theo Jackson leaving during the joint practices during a deep play. It looked like Jamal Adams was going to help out there and potentially at inside linebacker before his heartbreaking, season-ending injury at New York. Undrafted rookie Jacob Thomas has capitalized on the extra reps. I wanted to share an idea about how I believe the Vikings could use the preseason to create an advantage heading into the regular season. My suggestion is to treat the three preseason games as three additional opportunities to prepare our starting team before the games actually count. The NFL gives every team three games with no consequences to their regular-season record. I believe we should take full advantage of that. Rather than using preseason games primarily to determine the depth chart, I would use training camp practices for that purpose. Let players compete every day for their positions and establish who has earned the right to play. Then, when the preseason games begin, play our starters. What the opposing team chooses to do with its own lineup shouldn't really matter. Whether they play their starters, backups or third-string players, our objective should be preparing the Vikings. The value isn't necessarily who is lined up across from us. The value is getting our starting players into an actual NFL game environment. They get to experience the speed of the game, communication, timing, substitutions, play-calling, situational football and the process of playing together under game conditions. If we're destroying the other team, take the starters out. If we're up by a significant margin after three quarters, there is little reason to keep exposing them. Let the backups finish the game. But if we're not playing well, or the game is competitive, keep the starters on the field and use the opportunity. If everything is going well, you've gotten your starters meaningful reps and can get them out early. If things aren't going well, you have another quarter — and potentially another preseason game — to work on it before anything counts. You're essentially being given three games to identify and correct problems for free. I also believe this approach would make roster evaluation more effective. Instead of relying heavily on third-string players playing against third-string players, use training camp to evaluate those players against the Vikings' best players every day. A young offensive lineman shouldn't need four quarters against another team's third-string defensive line to determine whether he belongs. Coaches can learn a tremendous amount by watching him compete against the Vikings' starting defensive line throughout training camp. Then the preseason games can serve their most important purpose: Preparing the players who are actually expected to carry the team during the regular season. The Vikings have three games where a loss doesn't hurt the standings. I believe that's an opportunity that shouldn't be wasted. If we're dominating, pull the starters. If we're not, keep working. Either way, we're using those three games to make the team better before Week 1. Thank you for taking the time to consider my perspective. O'Connell prioritizes the joint practices as two of the best days of training camp to prepare first and second teamers for the regular season. The benefits include the number of snaps that can be accomplished each day, as well as going through some scripted and unscripted scenarios in a controlled environment that hopefully makes teams less susceptible to injuries. That means a preseason game at the end of a week of joint practices is likely to have third stringers or folks further down the depth chart in for most of the time, and the players who are suited up won't have gone through as many preparation reps, which are still few, during the week. Five years ago, Irv Smith, Jr., was entering his third pro season, and the Vikings had designed some plays to create mismatches for him. On the heels of catching 30 passes for 365 yards and five touchdowns in 2020, Smith was looking good in camp. For some reason, Smith was playing in the third preseason contest at Kansas City and suffered a season-ending injury. Fellow tight end Tyler Conklin went on to have a breakout season with 61 catches for 593 yards and three touchdowns, but I have wondered what the combo of Smith and Conklin could have done in 12 personnel and how that duplicity may have helped other aspects of the offense. O'Connell also believes in the importance of developing younger players. To that end, the preseason contests offer in-game reps, even though the scoreboard results don't matter. In a league where every regular-season game means so much, it's weird to think a team can have different goals not necessarily tied to the final score in the preseason, but that's likely going to be the case. Our defense is going to be our strength. Banks and Orange were very disruptive and will make for an awesome rotation. It is too early to throw J.J. out or even drop him to third-string. Who did J.J. play against? Who did Carson play against? Both of them will help us in my opinion. We have a good QB room. How did Walter Rouse play? He moved inside and did a great pancake block on that poor Baltimore DB. Every game in the NFC North will be tough. Skol to this season, Minnesota's defense is showing signs of being extremely difficult to deal with. On back-to-back days, the first team seemed to cause headaches throughout the Baltimore offense led by two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson. It's worth noting the highly elusive QB didn't seem to break pocket as much as he might in live action, but the team periods were one-sided on both days. Flores will be able to create multiple different packages and pressure looks with his system. The d-line looks capable of getting into the backfield from time to time on pass plays or for run stuffs, and the linebackers' blitzes could be quite a calling card, given what Blake Cashman and Eric Wilson have accomplished so far in this scheme. Andrew Van Ginkel is one of one for this system, and Dallas Turner's growth as an edge rusher was on full display Thursday against two-time Pro Bowl left tackle Ronnie Stanley. Elijah Williams Is the real deal. Please let him make the roster. Honestly, we have a good DL. Why did we draft more depth? I understand, but we need help other places and the DL wasn't it. How about edge and linebacker or corner. We miss a lot when you look back at draft. Banks looked like he should have gotten draft in Round 2 but not in the first round. What do you think? We're deep on WR, which also makes me think Jordan Addison won't get a deal. What is your opinion? Demond Claiborne looks good. A year under his belt, he would be a monster. Williams isn't the only player on Minnesota's roster who is easy to root for based on a vivacious personality. He's often flashing a smile to and from the locker room but also means business between the lines. How cool was it for the Jersey City native to record a sack in Preseason 1 just minutes from his hometown? I've already touched on the merits of Banks and Orange in earlier responses, but Minnesota parted ways with Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave in the offseason. That's two starting roles to fill, and Minnesota likes the projection of what Banks and Orange will accomplish. Other teams thought highly of Banks, and I don't believe he would have carried into the second round. It also appears that second-round pick Jake Golday is off to a great start of his career, too. While the Vikings d-line depth is probably stronger than other positions, it's a grueling position, and having a rotation to keep guys as fresh as possible is important. The trio of Justin Jefferson, Addison and Jauan Jennings could be one of the best in the NFL in 2026. Beyond that trio, the Vikings don't have a ton of proven regular-season experience. Price and Felton have had some strong days in training camp and are also likely to help significantly on special teams. Claiborne's bounce to the outside for an explosive touchdown run to end the second-team offense's 2-minute drill is an encouraging element to add to a room led by Aaron Jones, Sr., and Jordan Mason, even though Claiborne has been bottlenecked in the preseason to 52 yards on 20 carries. Many of those have been short-yardage between the tackles, which likely will never be his bread and butter, but he got the call based on who was available to play at various junctures of games. He's learning at every turn. It's also worth pointing out the Vikings aren't scheming their runs to try to attack opponents' defenses. This Dillon Bell is very impressive with his size and speed. If they can coach him up to catch the ball, his run after catch could be off the charts. Bell is listed at 6-foot, 209 pounds and has shown his ability to pop on a couple of run plays (two at New York for 27 yards with a long of 17). He's also caught six passes for 51 yards so far. title: Why Did Banking Stocks GS, JPM, BAC Surge To 52-Week Highs Today? - Stocktwits

(BAC) surged to annual highs after the banks posted stellar second-quarter earnings results that beat market expectations. GS stock led the climb among banking stocks, surging more than 9% after its record Q2 results triggered a buy-in. JPM stock rose 2.5% after its results surged past Wall Street expectations, while BAC stock also soared nearly 2% to a record high. GS stock climbed to a record high of $1,143.84 on Tuesday after the company reported record Q2 results that tore past analysts’ expectations. Goldman Sachs posted quarterly revenue of $20.98 billion, significantly higher than Wall Street's $16.4 billion estimate, according to Koyfin data. The investment bank also reported earnings of $15.91 per share, ahead of the $14.40 consensus estimate, while net income reached a record $6.32 billion for the quarter. The strong results were fueled by robust performance in investment banking, equities trading, and asset management, as companies continued to tap capital markets and pursue AI-related financing and strategic deals. "There's a lot of capital out there," CEO David Solomon said in an interview with CNBC on Tuesday. "I'm not concerned about the ability for the capital to be available for things that make sense." GS stock has surged nearly 25% so far this year. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ at the time of writing. JPM stock climbed to a 52-week high of $344.73 on Tuesday, driven by strong Q2 results that boosted investor interest in the company. The bank posted revenue of $57.35 billion versus a consensus estimate of $51.3 billion, while earnings per share (EPS) came in at $7.70 per share versus an expectation of $ 5.80 per share, based on Fiscal.ai data. JPMorgan delivered its strongest trading quarter on record, with trading revenue jumping 35% year over year to $12.1 billion. CEO Jamie Dimon said every business segment achieved record results, noting that market conditions remain favorable for sustained activity. Investment banking fees climbed 30% from a year earlier to $3.3 billion, marking their highest level since 2021, while net interest income rose 10% year over year to $25.6 billion. RKLB stock jumped nearly 3% on Tuesday, with shares also up nearly 2% overnight. Beck called SpaceX a “friendly rival” and said space companies often compete for one contract before working together on another: “You can be competing tooth and tail for a particular contract” and later team up to deliver it, he said. Rocket Lab can also benefit when rivals win as it supplies components such as reaction wheels, star trackers and solar panels.” “We can go head to head with a traditional space prime and then lose,” Beck said. “And then the next day, there’s a purchase order.” Beck called Rocket Lab an end-to-end space company spanning satellites, launch and services from orbit: “We build satellites, we launch them on our rockets and we provide services from space,” he said. Pointing to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Starlink model, Beck added: “They’re able to do all those things. And we’re able to do those too.” William Blair analyst Louie DiPalma recently named Rocket Lab and Blue Origin among the strongest challengers to SpaceX, though he said SpaceX still holds more than 90% of the launch market. Rocket Lab is advancing its competitive vertical integration strategy through its $8 billion acquisition of Iridium Communications, which would add a global network, spectrum, and recurring satellite service revenue. The company recently completed a full-duration burn of its Archimedes Vacuum engine, an important step toward the first flight of its reusable Neutron rocket. Rocket Lab said it was “critical preparation for Neutron’s first flight.” Beck has told Stocktwits earlier that Rocket Lab is “pushing very hard” to launch Neutron by the fourth quarter of 2026, while cautioning that the challenge is not merely reaching orbit but proving the rocket can return and be reused. “If we just had to go up, it’s super easy, we’d be in orbit by now,” he previously said. Rocket Lab also completed the U.S. Space Force’s Victus Haze mission, launching 16 hours and 42 minutes after receiving notice and completing spacecraft commissioning and proximity operations ahead of schedule. Could be an inflection point if positive.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. General Fusion Group Ltd. (GFUZ) made history on Monday, becoming the first pure-play nuclear fusion energy company to trade on a major public stock exchange. In an exclusive interview with Stocktwits, CEO Greg Twinney argued that fusion is not just a cleaner alternative to fission but is a fundamentally larger market opportunity. GFUZ stock surged 21% on its debut, added over 25% on Tuesday, and was trading about 2.5% lower in the overnight session. The Vancouver-based company, backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, went public through a SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, which provided General Fusion with approximately $150 million in cash. Earlier, Twinney told the Wall Street Journal that the funding is sufficient to meet the scientific milestones required by its demonstration machine. The listing arrives at a pivotal moment. Surging electricity demand driven by the AI boom, the global spread of electrification, and the energy appetite of large-scale computing has renewed urgency around new sources of firm, clean power. Fusion has attracted growing investment and government attention as a potential long-term answer. According to the Financial Times, the number of private fusion companies has more than doubled over the past five years, intensifying competition at a time when the technology is still roughly a decade from commercialization. General Fusion is targeting its first commercial plant around 2035. Twinney's bull case for fusion starts with what it doesn't produce. Unlike fission, fusion does not generate long-lived radioactive waste, does not use fuels that could be weaponized, and carries no risk of a meltdown. "Fusion is just inherently safe. We're not needing to engineer safety into it in the same way that you need to with fission," he told Stocktwits. "When fusion fails, it kind of just fails safely and there's not really any fallout from that." That safety profile has a direct commercial implication: regulators around the world are moving to govern fusion "in a much lighter way" than conventional nuclear, Twinney said, which he believes creates the potential to site fusion plants closer to population centers and industrial demand. That's a significant advantage over fission, which requires remote, heavily secured facilities. "We get all the benefits that fission can provide without the downsides," he said. There's another significant advantage. Fusion reactors primarily use deuterium, which can be extracted from seawater and is "massively abundant." The other component, tritium, is rarer in nature but can be bred through the interaction of a neutron and lithium. Fission, by contrast, relies on uranium and other finite sources. "The overall market size because of the safety profile and the abundance of fuel in fusion is much bigger than fission," Twinney said. While advanced nuclear companies such as Oklo Inc. (OKLO) and NuScale Power Corp. (SMR) are often thought of as being closer to commercialization than fusion technology, Twinney said that the gap may not be as large as investors assume. While the road to commercialization for fusion technology has its challenges, including achieving reactor durability, tritium fuel breeding, economic viability, and the ability to efficiently extract and convert fusion energy into electricity, he argues small modular reactor (SMR) timelines also struggle with regulatory hurdles that can make timelines less predictable than they appear today. "I know that the timelines for SMRs, which can be very unpredictable due to regulations and those types of things, [are] probably not that different," he said. According to Twinney, the combination of abundant fuel supplies and a lighter regulatory framework could ultimately enable fusion to scale faster than conventional nuclear technologies once commercial viability has been demonstrated. However, Twinney does not view fusion and fission as mutually exclusive technologies. "They will be complementing each other," he said. "And I think that fusion kind of rounds out the nuclear circle if you think about it that way," he added. When asked about criticism from former Commonwealth Fusion Systems CTO Dan Brunner, who, in a recent interview with the Financial Times, said General Fusion's commercialization timeline was "very hard to believe," Twinney said the company’s timelines were based on real experimental results from its Lawson Machine 26. The machine is designed to demonstrate that plasma can be heated through mechanical compression rather than superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers, he said, adding that the company's early results validated the operating principles behind its MTF approach that are “not based on fiction or papers being written.” The timelines “are based on our real results from machines that we have built and operated and then eventually written papers on. But those are real results papers, not theoretical papers,” he said. Twinney also emphasized that General Fusion's approach could offer a cost advantage over many competing technologies. While many other fusion developers rely on expensive superconducting magnets, high-powered lasers, or advanced materials that have yet to be proven at commercial scale, General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) system uses mechanical compression and a liquid-lithium wall that can protect reactor components from neutron damage, help with breeding tritium fuel, and absorbing fusion energy as heat that can be converted into electricity using conventional steam turbines. In an earlier interview with Stocktwits, Chief Strategy Officer Megan Wilson had also pointed to the economic advantages of MTF, which eliminate the need for expensive magnets, targets, lasers, or exotic, not-yet-invented materials. The technology also eliminates the need for frequent replacement of components damaged by neutron exposure, she had said. “Our plants are designed to be cost-competitive compared to coal, steam, and natural gas,” she had said then. “They are expected to deliver four times as much energy per unit of fuel as fission, without long-lived radioactive waste, positioning them as the superior nuclear technology for sustainable growth.” By avoiding costly magnets and lasers and using existing industrial technologies, Twinney said he believes General Fusion has a clearer path to building an economically viable power plant, as the company’s design has from the beginning aimed to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. "What we are trying to do at General Fusion, and our power plant design from the beginning, has been we want to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. Not just demonstrate a bunch of fusion, but actually avoid the barriers to commercializing it," he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around GFUZ stock is ‘bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volumes. title: GS rates may correct on US move to support bonds - BusinessWorld Online
content: RATES of the government securities (GS) to be offered this week may end mixed amid increased volume as the Treasury is set to auction off cash management bills anew, and with the United States’ effort to support long-dated  bonds seen to stem the rise in yields. Investing On Monday, the Bureau of the Treasury (BTr) will auction off up to P80 billion in short-term securities. Broken down, it will offer P20 billion in 35-day cash management bills (CMBs). It last sold CMBs on July 20. Meanwhile, it will auction off up to P60 billion in Treasury bills (T-bills). Specifically, the Treasury will look raise P20-25 billion from 91-day papers, P15-20 billion via 182-day securities, and P7-15 billion through 364-day debt. Investing On Tuesday, the government is targeting to borrow P30 billion from reissued seven-year Treasury bonds (T-bonds) with a remaining life of three years and one month. Debt yields could be mixed or slightly lower, tracking movements at the secondary market, after the US Treasury announced they will increase buybacks of long-term US government bonds to help bring down yields after a global rout, Rizal Commercial  Banking Corp. Chief Economist Michael L. Ricafort said in a Viber message. This could help reduce borrowing costs around the world, he said. “The government securities (GS) market traded 3 basis points (bps) lower as it tracked US Treasury movements as US Treasury Secretary Bessent announced a surprise increase in long-term  bond buybacks. Nonetheless, players used the opportunity to lighten positions,” a trader said in an e-mail. “Price action was generally two-way but offers were noticeably heavy.” Investing As a result, the trader said the reissued bonds to be sold this week could see good demand and fetch rates from 6.775% to 6.8%. At the secondary market on Thursday, yields on the 35- and 91-day tenors rose by 3.56 bps and 5.39 bps week on week to close at 4.7644% and 5.0025%, according to the PHP Bloomberg Valuation Service Reference Rates published on the Philippine Dealing System website. Meanwhile, the 182-day and 364-day T-bills went down by 1.73 bps and 5.78 bps to end at 5.3212% and 5.6593%. For its part, the seven-year bond went up by 3.84 bps to end at 7.2124%, while the three-year tenor, the closest to the remaining life of the bond series on offer on Tuesday, inched up by 1.23 bps to close at 6.6877%. Mr. Ricafort added that inflation concerns could also affect yield movements as the Middle East war continues. Bets on the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) policy move this week and direction moving forward could likewise be on the market’s radar, he said. The government last offered 35-day cash management bills on July 20, where it raised P20 billion as planned at an average rate of 4.816%. The Treasury began offering CMBs again in June for the first time since the pandemic to manage short-term liquidity needs amid elevated interest rates. Meanwhile, last week, the BTr raised P54.8 billion from the T-bills it auctioned off, above the P46 billion on offer as total tenders reached P167.016 billion. This came as the government doubled its acceptance of noncompetitive bids for the six-month and one-year tenors to P12 billion and P5.6 billion, respectively. Broken down, the Treasury borrowed P24 billion as planned via the 91-day T-bills as bids for the tenor reached P42.7 billion. The three-month paper fetched an average rate of 5.008%, up by 1.3 bps from the previous week. Bids accepted had yields from 4.9% to 5.026%. For the 182-day debt, the government raised P21 billion, above the P15-billion plan as tenders hit P84.09 billion. The average yield on the six-month T-bill was at 5.442%, dropping by 10.3 bps from the last auction. Tenders awarded had rates from 5.4% to 5.463%. Lastly, the BTr sold P9.8 billion in 364-day securities, higher than the P7-billion program, as demand for the tenor totaled P40.226 billion. The one-year paper fetched an average rate of 5.613%, declining by 1.8 bps week on week. Accepted yields ranged from 5.595% to 5.633%. Meanwhile, the reissued seven-year T-bonds to be offered on Tuesday were last auctioned off on July 28, where the government raised a total of P40 billion, or P30 billion via the regular auction and P10 billion from a tap facility offering. The papers fetched an average yield of 7.217%, above the 7% coupon rate. The Treasury plans to raise P330 billion from the domestic market this month, or P200 billion via T-bills and P130 billion through T-bonds. The government borrows from local and foreign sources to help  finance its budget deficit, which is capped at P1.659 trillion or 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. — Aaron Michael C. Sy

title: A fine of 1.027 billion won has been confirmed for GS Retail, which has passed the burden on supplie.. - 매일경제

A fine of 1.027 billion won has been confirmed for GS Retail, which has passed the burden on suppliers by transferring promotional costs. According to the legal community on the 23rd, the Supreme Court Department 3 (Chief Justice Roh Kyung-pil) recently confirmed its ruling against the plaintiff in a lawsuit filed by GS Retail against the Fair Trade Commission for cancellation, including a corrective order. On January 26, 2022, the FTC imposed a fine of 1.027 billion won along with a correction order and notification order, saying GS Retail violated the Large Distribution Business Act. GS Retail has three major violations of the law. ▲Burden of promotional expenses such as free gift events between January 2015 and November 2018 to the supplier without written agreement (violation of Clause 1 and Clause 2 of Article 11 of the Large Distribution Business Act) ▲Return of many products from April 2017 to October 2019 after receiving only a request for export from the supplier (violation of Clause 1 of Article 10) ▲In January 2018 and June 2020, broadcasters and celebrities belonging to suppliers were required to perform guest or model duties for their home shopping broadcasts without a written agreement on the terms of dispatch (violation of Clause 1 of Article 12). According to the law, large retailers cannot return products purchased directly. The supplier shall voluntarily request a return by attaching objective evidence in writing that the return benefits them directly. This is to prevent large companies from handing over inventory to suppliers. Receiving personnel from suppliers is also prohibited to block 'gapjil'. Only if the terms of dispatch are agreed in writing in advance are limited. GS Retail filed a lawsuit saying it cannot accept the FTC's fine. The FTC disposition had the same effect as the first trial decision, so it was immediately judged by the second trial. At the trial, GS Retail claimed that it was a voluntary return because it received a request for export from suppliers, and that the broadcaster was not a "employee" who was prohibited by law from being dispatched. He also said that even if the law is violated, the FTC's penalty is excessive. The court did not accept it. The second trial court pointed out, "The violation of the ban on product returns is worth about 1.8 billion won, which is by no means small," adding, "There is a high concern that large retailers will use their superior position in the transaction to provide disadvantages to their counterparts by unfairly taking back their products, thereby entrenching abnormal trading practices and hindering fair trading." Considering that the proportion of violations among all events is small, the act of transferring sales promotion costs was also judged not to be excessive by setting the penalty amount at 175 million won.
